name: Effects of Sleep Deprivation
what: This subtopic covers the three categories of effects that result from sleep deprivation: affective (emotional), behavioural (action-based), and cognitive (mental process-based). Each category contains multiple specific changes that impair daily functioning.
why: The study design explicitly requires students to analyse affective, behavioural, and cognitive effects of sleep deprivation. These three categories appear consistently in exam short-answer and extended-response questions and must be distinguished clearly.

items.title: I can define affective effects of sleep deprivation and list specific examples
items.what: Affective effects refer to changes in emotional functioning that arise from sleep deprivation. These include increased irritability, heightened sensitivity, amplified emotional responses, and difficulty accurately judging the emotions of others.
items.why: Affective effects are distinct from cognitive and behavioural effects, and examiners expect students to correctly categorise emotional changes under the affective domain rather than the cognitive domain.
items.example: After only 5 hours of sleep, Starr the nurse finds herself snapping at patients over minor issues and misreading a colleague's neutral expression as hostile. These are affective effects: increased irritability and impaired emotion recognition.

items.title: I can define behavioural effects of sleep deprivation and list specific examples
items.what: Behavioural effects refer to changes in actions and the ability to control them due to sleep deprivation. These include slowed reaction time, reduced motor control, increased clumsiness, involuntary microsleeps, diminished social functioning, and reduced efficiency when completing tasks.
items.why: Behavioural effects are observable and often carry safety consequences, which is why they appear in scenario questions involving driving, workplace accidents, and physical tasks. Correctly attributing these to the behavioural domain is required.
items.example: Evan, who slept only 5 hours during a 29-hour flight, drops items repeatedly during his first day back at work and takes twice as long as usual to complete a simple filing task. These are behavioural effects: reduced motor control and reduced efficiency.

items.title: I can define cognitive effects of sleep deprivation and list specific examples
items.what: Cognitive effects refer to changes in mental processes that arise from sleep deprivation. These include reduced concentration, lapses in attention, impaired short-term memory, impaired decision-making and problem-solving, diminished creativity, reduced retention of information, irrational thinking, and impaired visual and spatial ability.
items.why: Cognitive effects directly affect academic and occupational performance and are the category most likely to be confused with affective effects. Knowing that memory, attention, and decision-making are cognitive, not emotional, is a common exam distinction.
items.example: After 24 hours without sleep, Solomon struggles to recall information he studied earlier, keeps re-reading the same question on his university test without processing it, and makes a careless arithmetic error he would not normally make. These are cognitive effects.

items.title: I can explain what microsleeps are and categorise them correctly as a behavioural effect
items.what: Microsleeps are involuntary, brief lapses into sleep lasting only a few seconds, during which the individual has no awareness that they have fallen asleep. They are classified as a behavioural effect of sleep deprivation because they involve an uncontrolled change in action.
items.why: Microsleeps carry significant safety risks, particularly when driving or operating machinery, and are a specific term that examiners expect students to define precisely. Misclassifying microsleeps as a cognitive effect is a common error.
items.example: A truck driver who has been awake for 20 hours experiences a 3-second microsleep while driving on the highway. During those 3 seconds, at 100 km/h, the vehicle travels approximately 83 metres with no conscious control from the driver.

items.title: I can describe the long-term health risks associated with chronic sleep deprivation
items.what: Chronic (long-term) sleep deprivation is associated with an increased risk of raised blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity, lowered immunity, and increased risk of depression and anxiety. These are distinct from the acute effects seen after one night of poor sleep.
items.why: While not always the primary exam focus, long-term effects contextualise why sleep is important for mental and physical wellbeing beyond a single night, and they support extended-response questions about sleep and health.
items.example: A person who consistently sleeps only 5 hours per night for several years faces a measurably elevated risk of cardiovascular disease and depression compared to someone who consistently gets 8 hours, even if their daily impairments seem mild.
